These agents are vertically stacked with shared encoder layers and an aggregator module at the end. At the bottom, each agent receives an input time series represented by a dashed-line waveform. This input is first passed through an 'Embed' layer, then sequentially processed by multiple 'l-th Encoder Layer' blocks (for higher-level abstraction) and 'i-st Encoder Layer' blocks (for lower-level features), before being fed into the respective 'Agent Head'. The Agent Heads output the estimated component (Trend, Seasonality, etc.) as a waveform or statistical summary, which is then projected to form the final future series forecast. The outputs from all four agents are aggregated via a central 'Aggregator' module, which contains two components: a 'Global Voter' (dashed box) and an 'Agent Confidence Estimator' (dashed box). The Aggregator's output feeds into a 'Projection' block that generates the final forecasted time series, denoted as Ŷ. Arrows indicate data flow: inputs ascend through encoder layers to agent heads, while outputs from agent heads feed into the aggregator. Red arrows show cross-agent communication between encoder layers, suggesting information exchange or attention mechanisms. The entire structure is designed to decompose complex time series into interpretable components, model them independently, and combine predictions for improved accuracy.

Each format displays how 8 complex numbers are stored as either 8 complex pairs or 5 complex numbers plus 3 float numbers. A red arrow points from this section to the next, indicating a transition to computation. The second section, 'Butterfly Operation Diagram', shows a hierarchical decomposition of a 16-point FFT (16-FFT) into stages of 2-FFT, 4-FFT, and finally an 8-FFT at the center, depicted as an orange box. The third section, titled 'Complex-to-Complex FFT (Red Line in FFT-16)' and colored blue, expands one of the red paths into explicit mathematical operations involving complex inputs (e.g., a₂ + b₂j) and outputs (x₂, x₆, etc.), using twiddle factors W_N^k. The final section, 'Float-to-Float IFFT (Red Line in FFT-16)', continues the real-valued flow, showing how real inputs are transformed back into complex outputs using inverse trigonometric relationships. The entire layout follows a top-down workflow from storage format to butterfly decomposition to detailed arithmetic expansions, emphasizing the in-place real-domain FFT design.

visual_intent: Figure 4: Overview of the proposed architecture for disentangling semantic and visual features from a frozen diffusion backbone $\Phi$ . Inconsistent regions between the input image pairs are indicated by binary masks (left). The semantic branch (blue) encourages the features of corresponding semantic points in both images, $P _ { 1 }$ and $P _ { 2 }$ , to align. In the visual branch (yellow), we bring visually consistent points outside the inpainted regions, $P _ { 1 } ^ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ and $P _ { 2 } ^ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ , closer together, while pushing apart features at inconsistent points inside the inpainted regions, $P _ { 1 } ^ { \mathrm { i n } }$ and $P _ { 2 } ^ { \mathrm { i n } }$ .
golden_prompt: The diagram illustrates a neural network architecture designed to disentangle semantic and visual features from an input pair of inconsistent images using a frozen diffusion backbone Φ. On the left, two example images of motorcycles are shown side-by-side, each with a black square mask indicating an inconsistent region; this serves as input. These inputs feed into two parallel processing branches: a blue semantic aggregation branch and a yellow visual aggregation branch, both rooted in the same diffusion model Φ. The semantic branch processes features through a series of blue residual blocks (labeled ψ^s) which aggregate semantic information, then outputs disentangled semantic features S1 and S2. These features are combined via a dot block (⊕) to compute semantic similarity D^s_12, which is then passed through an indexing operation [·] and fed into a cross-entropy loss CE labeled L_s. The visual branch processes features through yellow residual blocks (ψ^v) to extract visual features V1 and V2, which are similarly combined via a dot block (⊕) to compute visual similarity D^v_12. This similarity is then split into two paths: one path uses an indexing operation [·] on output points P1^out and P2^out to compute a cross-entropy loss CE labeled L_out_v, encouraging alignment of visually consistent regions outside the masked areas. The other path applies a negation operation (⊖) to the same similarity score and feeds it into another cross-entropy loss CE labeled L_in_v, which pushes apart features at inconsistent points inside the masked regions (P1^in and P2^in). A legend at the bottom identifies visual elements: blue blocks represent residual blocks, yellow blocks represent residual blocks, circular dot blocks represent dot operations, square brackets [·] represent indexing, a circle with a minus sign ⊖ represents negation, and green CE boxes represent cross-entropy loss functions. The overall structure is a dual-branch architecture where semantic consistency is enforced across masked regions, while visual consistency is optimized both within and outside those regions, enabling disentanglement of feature representations.

visual_intent: Figure 3: Overall framework of the proposed MixPrompt for multimodal semantic segmentation. The RGB input is processed by an RGB-pretrained segmentation model, while the auxiliary input is processed by a lightweight prompting module. In the prompting module, the initial prompt is derived from the early blocks of the pretrained RGB model (Section 3). At each stage, auxiliary features are projected into multiple subspaces and subsequently mixed to align with the RGB features by mixed prompting modules (Section 4.2). The fused features are used as prompt and are fed back into the main branch. Finally, the segmentation mask is generated by a prediction head based on the output features of the main branch. During training, only the lightweight prompting module and the prediction head are trainable, ensuring the parameter efficiency of the proposed framework.
golden_prompt:
The diagram illustrates the overall framework of MixPrompt for multimodal semantic segmentation, structured into two primary processing streams: a main RGB backbone branch and a lightweight mixed prompting module, which integrates auxiliary input features. The layout is horizontally organized with the RGB input stream at the top, the auxiliary input stream below it, and the prompting module spanning beneath both, feeding back into the main backbone. The final prediction head is positioned at the far right.

The top stream begins with an 'RGB Input' image (shown as a real-world scene) entering a 'Patch Embedding' block. This feeds into a sequence of stacked 'Block 1', 'Block 2', ..., up to 'Block N', forming the main backbone. Each block is connected via point-wise add operations (indicated by a circle with a plus sign), suggesting residual connections. A small snowflake icon next to Block N indicates this part is a frozen module. The output of the last backbone block is passed to a 'Head' module (marked with a fire icon indicating it's trainable), which generates the final 'Prediction' (a color-coded segmentation map).

The bottom-left auxiliary input stream starts with an 'Aux. Input' (a heatmap-like image) entering a 'Feature Extractor'. Its output then sequentially passes through 'Prompter 1', 'Prompter 2', ..., up to 'Prompter N', forming the mixed prompting module. These prompters are colored light purple and marked with a fire icon, indicating they are trainable. This entire prompting module is labeled 'Mixed Prompter'.

A separate 'Prompt Initialization' block is shown at the bottom-left, taking input from an 'RGB Pretrained Model' (depicted as stacked convolutional layers) and producing an initial prompt vector e₀, which is fed into the first 'Down' layer of the mixed prompting module. The mixed prompting module itself consists of a series of 'Down' layers (triangular shapes) that progressively reduce spatial dimensions, followed by a central 'Mixing Layer' (a rectangular box with dashed borders). After mixing, the features pass through 'Up' layers (inverted triangular shapes) to restore resolution. The outputs from the 'Down' layers are concatenated (indicated by a 'S' symbol) and combined with the backbone features via point-wise addition (circle with plus sign) before being fed into the next 'Down' layer. The final output of the mixed prompting module is denoted as eᵢ, which is then added to the corresponding backbone feature at each stage.

The two streams are interconnected: the output of each 'Prompter' (e.g., Prompter 1) is connected to the 'Block 1' via a point-wise addition operation, and similarly, Prompter 2 connects to Block 2, etc. This feedback mechanism allows the auxiliary prompts to dynamically adjust the backbone features at each stage. The 'Mixed Prompting Module' also receives the backbone feature hᵢ₋₁ from the previous stage and outputs eᵢ to be added to the current backbone feature.

A legend on the right side clarifies the visual symbols: a snowflake represents a frozen module, a fire icon represents a trainable module, a circle with a plus sign denotes point-wise addition, and a 'S' symbol indicates concatenation. The caption explains that during training, only the lightweight prompting module and the prediction head are trainable, ensuring parameter efficiency.

visual_intent: Figure 2: The overview of T2MIR. (a) Overall pipeline: we substitute the feedforward layer in causal transformer blocks with two parallel MoE layers and concatenate their outputs to feed into the next layer. (b) Token-wise MoE: it automatically captures distinct semantic features within the multi-modal $( s , a , r )$ inputs, and uses $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { b a l a n c e } }$ as regularization loss to avoid tokens from all modalities collapsing onto minority experts. (c) Task-wise MoE: it assigns diverse tasks to specialized experts, and includes a contrastive learning loss $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { c o n t r a s t i v e } }$ to enhance task-wise routing via more precise capture of task-relevant information, where $\tau _ { i }$ is the query and $\tau _ { i ^ { * } } / \tau _ { i ^ { \prime } }$ are positive/negative keys.
golden_prompt: The T2MIR Framework diagram is divided into three main sections labeled (a), (b), and (c), each describing a component of the model's architecture. Section (a), titled 'Overall pipeline', shows the core structure of the model: starting from an 'Embedding' layer, the output feeds into a 'Multi-Head Attention' block followed by a 'Layer Norm'. Above this, a 'Token-MoE' block and a 'Task-MoE' block are shown in parallel, both connected to an 'Action Head'. The 'Token-MoE' and 'Task-MoE' blocks are connected via a 'Layer Norm' and then merge their outputs before feeding into the 'Action Head'. The 'Action Head' has an arrow pointing to a loss function labeled 'L(θ)', which also receives input from the 'Token-MoE' and 'Task-MoE' blocks. The 'Action Head' is also connected to a 'Router_task' block in section (c) via a dashed line. The 'Router_task' block in section (c) takes inputs τ₀ through τₘ and routes them to different experts. Section (b), titled 'Token-wise MoE', shows a 'Router_token' block receiving inputs s₀ through s_T and a₀ through a_T, along with r₀ through r_T. These inputs are routed to different experts (expert₁ through expert_K₁) based on top-k selection (top1 and top2). The outputs from these experts are combined using a 'Concatenation' operation, indicated by a cross symbol, and fed back into the 'Router_token' block. A dotted arrow labeled 'L_balance' connects the outputs of the experts to the 'Router_token' block, indicating a balancing loss. Section (c), titled 'Task-wise MoE', shows a 'Router_task' block taking inputs τ_i, τ_i*, and τ_i' (where τ_i* is a positive key and τ_i' is a negative key) and routing them to different experts. The 'Router_task' block is connected to a 'Momentum Router_task' block, which also takes inputs τ_i, τ_i*, and τ_i'. The 'Momentum Router_task' block is connected to the 'Router_task' block via a dashed line. The 'Router_task' block is also connected to a contrastive loss function labeled 'L_contrastive', which receives inputs from the 'Router_task' block and the 'Momentum Router_task' block. The diagram includes a legend at the bottom left corner explaining the symbols used: a cross symbol represents concatenation, a plus symbol represents residual connection, solid arrows represent higher gate weights, and dashed arrows represent lower gate weights. The overall layout is organized with section (a) in the center, section (b) on the left, and section (c) on the right, with clear visual separation between the components.

visual_intent: Figure 1: Pipeline of MoE-Gyro framework. During inference, a low-quality signal stream is segmented, routed by a gate to suitable expert, and the enhanced outputs are concatenated to form the final signal. During training, both experts are optimised in a fully self-supervised manner on a shared MAE backbone, each equipped with task-specific masking, attention, and loss mechanisms.
golden_prompt:
The figure illustrates the MoE-Gyro framework, divided into two main sections: the Inference Pipeline (left, green-bordered) and the Training Pipeline (center, blue-bordered), with an auxiliary GD-Attention module (right, purple-bordered). The overall layout is horizontal, with the inference pipeline on the left, training pipeline in the center, and the GD-Attention module on the right, connected via dashed red arrows indicating supervision signals. A legend box at the bottom-right defines visual encoding: orange squares represent threshold masks, light gray squares complementary masks, orange rectangles latent tokens, blue squares valid outputs, dark gray squares invalid outputs, solid black arrows weight share, and dashed red arrows supervision.

In the Inference Pipeline, a noisy input signal (green waveform) enters from the bottom-left, labeled 'Noise' and 'Clip'. This signal is fed into a 'Router' (green rounded rectangle) which routes it to one of two experts: 'ORE' (orange rounded rectangle) or 'DE' (blue rounded rectangle). The Router receives input from a 'Gate' (green rounded rectangle) and a 'Concat' block (green rounded rectangle). The Gate takes inputs from ORE and DE, and its output feeds into Concat. The Concat block combines outputs from ORE and DE, then passes them through the Gate before routing back to the Router. The final reconstructed signal (orange waveform) emerges from the top, labeled 'Reconstruction', and undergoes 'Denoise' processing. The entire inference section is enclosed in a green rounded rectangle labeled 'Inference Pipeline'.

The Training Pipeline is split into two parallel expert branches: 'Over-range Reconstruction Expert' (top, orange-bordered) and 'Denoise Expert' (bottom, blue-bordered). Both are trained on a shared MAE backbone (green waveform input). The Over-range Reconstruction Expert begins with an 'Encoder' (orange trapezoid) that processes the input signal, followed by a 'Decoder' (purple trapezoid) containing 'Gaussian Decay Attention' and 'Add & Norm & FFN' modules. The Denoise Expert consists of two parallel streams, each with an 'Enc.' (light blue trapezoid) and 'Dec.' (dark blue trapezoid) module, processing the input signal after 'FFT + Noise' transformation. Both expert branches feed into a 'Loss Calculator' (blue dashed rectangle) that computes loss based on the outputs. The Loss Calculator connects back to both experts via dashed red arrows, indicating supervision. The outputs of both experts also connect to the GD-Attention module via dashed red arrows.

The GD-Attention module (purple-bordered) takes four keys K1-K4 (purple squares) and a query Q1 (purple square). It computes attention scores using the softmax function: Softmax(Q1Kj^T / sqrt(dk)) * d_ij^2 / 2σ^2, where σ is a parameter. The attention scores are then used to compute weighted outputs A11-A14 (purple squares), which are labeled as 'Valid output' or 'Invalid output' based on color (blue or dark gray). These outputs are connected back to the Loss Calculator via dashed red arrows, indicating supervision. The GD-Attention module is connected to the Over-range Reconstruction Expert via a dashed red arrow, indicating supervision. The entire Training Pipeline is enclosed in a blue rounded rectangle labeled 'Training Pipeline'.

Each Matryoshka sequence goes through MoME, which can be placed parallel to multiple modules within each LLM layer (parallel to the MHSA module in the Figure). Each MoME module comprises a top- $k$ router, which sparsely activates a subset of routed experts, and a pool of shared experts to capture scale-invariant knowledge.

The layout is divided into three main vertical sections: input processing on the left, the MoME module in the center-right, and the LLM context on the top-right. A legend on the far left defines token types using color-coded blocks: blue for Text Tokens, purple for Audio Tokens, green for Visual Tokens, and multi-colored blocks for Audio-Visual Tokens, with specific rates (e.g., (A,V) rates = (16,5) or (4,2)) indicating token counts. The bottom-left section shows raw inputs: an audio waveform fed into an Audio Encoder, and a video frame sequence fed into a Video Encoder. visual_intent: Figure 2: The overall pipeline of ComGS framework. (a) The reconstruction process starts from the first frame initialized using vanilla 3DGS [17]. Subsequent frames are organized into groups of frames (GoFs). For non-key frames, (b) we begin with a motion-sensitive keypoint selection using a viewspace gradient difference strategy, (c) and utilizes an adaptive motion-driven mechanism to control neighboring points motion. For key frames, (d) an error-aware correction strategy is introduced to mitigate the error accumulation across frames.

The top branch, under "Non-key frame reconstruction," details the motion-sensitive keypoint selection and adaptive motion-driven mechanism. It begins with two adjacent frames (t-1 and t), represented as images with overlaid yellow Gaussians, feeding into a "Viewspace Gradient Difference" module. visual_intent: Figure 1: The overall framework for communication-constrained MARL. It can be divided into three main steps: $\textcircled{1}$ Distinguishing between lossy and lossless messages by constructing communication link priors; $\textcircled{2}$ Shaping the global reward through learning Du-MIE for constrained communication; $\textcircled{3}$ Stably optimizing multi-agent policies based on MARL algorithms.
golden_prompt: The diagram presents a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework designed for environments with communication constraints. The layout is divided into three main vertical sections, each corresponding to one of the three steps outlined in the caption: (1) constructing communication link priors, (2) shaping global rewards via Du-MIE learning, and (3) stabilizing policy optimization. On the left, an 'Ideal environment' and 'Real environment' are shown as abstracted landscapes, connected by an arrow labeled 'Communication Link Unknown Function', indicating uncertainty in the channel. Below this, a 'Multi-agent' group of robot icons interacts with an 'Agent i' node, which sends 'Messages' to the central processing unit. A dashed box labeled 'Agent i' contains a message buffer showing sequences of messages $m_t^{i}$ and observations $o_t^i$, with arrows indicating message flow from previous time steps. A key distinction is made between 'Lossy message' (light beige) and 'Lossless message' (darker beige), visually represented in the message buffer. An upward arrow from the message buffer points to a 'Communication Link Prediction Function', which is depicted as a bell-shaped curve, representing the learned prior distribution. This step is marked with a red circle labeled ①. In the center-right section, two parallel neural network modules are shown: a 'JSD estimator' and a 'CLUB estimator'. Each has inputs from the message buffer ($m_t^{ji}, a_t^i, a_k^i$) and outputs to loss functions $I_{JSD}$ and $I_{CLUB}$. The JSD estimator uses parameters $\theta_1$, while the CLUB estimator uses $\theta_2$. Both estimators feed into a 'Message-Action Encoder' and 'Action Prediction Network', respectively. These networks are connected to a 'Replay Buffer' (a cylindrical icon) that stores trajectories $\langle o_t^i, M_t^i, l_t^i \rangle$ and feeds them back into the network via a blue arrow labeled 'Trajectory'. The output of the networks is combined using '+' and '-' operators to form a final reward signal $r_t \rightarrow \tilde{r}_t$. This section is marked with a red circle labeled ②. The third section, marked with a red circle labeled ③, shows the 'Replay Buffer' feeding into a 'MARL algorithm' module, which is represented as a blue dashed rectangle containing the equation $\mathcal{L}_{MARL}(\theta_Q, \theta_\pi)$, indicating the loss function used for policy optimization. The entire structure is interconnected with arrows indicating data flow and dependencies, forming a closed-loop learning system where agents learn to communicate effectively under bandwidth constraints.

visual_intent: Figure 2: Pipeline for Synthetic Data Generation and Curation in VTS-V. Our data construction process consists of three stages: (1) generating multi-step reasoning trajectories with visual tool calls, (2) filtering out incorrect trajectories using an LLM-as-a-judge framework, and (3) creating contrastive (correct vs. incorrect) trajectory pairs for multi-step DPO training.
golden_prompt:
The diagram illustrates a three-stage pipeline for synthetic data generation and curation in VTS-V, designed to train models on multi-step reasoning with visual tools. The global layout is horizontal and sequential, progressing from left to right through three main phases: trajectory generation, error filtering, and data pair creation. Each stage is visually demarcated by distinct blocks and arrows indicating flow.

In the first stage, "Multi-Step Reasoning with Visual Token Scaling" (VTS Inference), a question is posed at the top left: "What team does the player catching the baseball play for?" Below this, two parallel paths diverge: one labeled "Chosen" and another "Rejected." The "Chosen" path shows a successful reasoning sequence where the model identifies the player, zooms into the uniform, and correctly reads "TEXAS" to conclude the player plays for the Texas team. This path includes three steps with visual token scaling actions (grounding_action, zoom_action, ocr_action) and corresponding image crops (image1, image2). The "Rejected" path demonstrates an incorrect reasoning attempt: the model tries depth maps, OCR, and image-text similarity, but fails to extract text or find a match, concluding incorrectly with "Boston Red Sox." Both paths end with a result box showing the final answer and a green checkmark for correct or red X for incorrect.

From these two paths, arrows lead to a central "LLM as Judge" module, which evaluates whether the model's prediction matches the given answer. A feedback loop connects back to the "Chosen" and "Rejected" paths: if the LLM judges the answer correct (green check), it confirms the trajectory; if incorrect (red X), it triggers "Error Induction" to generate an incorrect reasoning path. The "Error Induction" block contains a failed example where the model incorrectly concludes the player plays for the Boston Red Sox based on a similarity score, despite the correct answer being "Texas team." This incorrect path is then used to create a contrastive pair.

The second stage, "Filtering Incorrect Trajectories," uses the LLM judge to validate trajectories. Correct trajectories (green check) are retained, while incorrect ones (red X) are flagged for error induction. The third stage, "Creating Contrastive Pairs," generates SFT Data by pairing the correct trajectory with the induced incorrect one. This is shown as a box labeled "SFT Data" receiving input from both the correct and incorrect paths. The entire process is designed to produce high-quality, contrastive training data for multi-step DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) training, enabling models to learn from both correct and erroneous reasoning paths. The diagram uses consistent visual elements: rectangular boxes for modules, arrows for directional flow, colored circles (green for correct, red for incorrect) for judgment outcomes, and text annotations to explain actions and results.

We first input the structured table, question, and answer into DeepSeek to generate a reasoning trace, and apply reject sampling to improve data quality. path_to_gt_image: images/Multiverse Your Language Models Secretly Decide How to Parallelize and Merge Generation_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 6: Multiverse co-design data (Multiverse $1K$ ), algorithm (Multiverse Attention), and system (Multiverse Engine) to enable real-world reasoning capabilities through a rapid shift from AR-LLMs.
golden_prompt:
The figure presents two complementary diagrams illustrating the "Multiverse" framework's core components: (b) Multiverse Attention and (c) Multiverse Engine. Together, they depict a parallel, multi-path reasoning system designed to enhance LLMs' ability to handle complex, multi-step tasks by dynamically managing multiple reasoning paths simultaneously.

In diagram (b), "Multiverse Attention", a grid-like structure visualizes the hierarchical decomposition of a reasoning task into multiple parallel paths. The vertical axis represents the task's logical structure, starting from a root goal node at the top, followed by branching path nodes, and concluding with a final conclusion node at the bottom. Each row corresponds to a specific level of the task hierarchy, labeled with tags such as <Goal>, <Path>, and <Con>. The horizontal axis represents the sequence of steps or tokens within each path, with each cell indicating a token position. The grid is divided into distinct regions: the leftmost column contains the hierarchical tags; the middle section shows the progression of paths, with each path represented by a diagonal band of cells labeled with its respective path identifier (e.g., p1, p2, p3); and the rightmost column contains the final conclusion. The bottom of the grid includes a formula: max(p1, p2, p3, p4) + 1, indicating the maximum path length plus one, which determines the total number of tokens needed for the entire process. This structure enables the model to attend to different parts of the reasoning graph simultaneously across all active paths.

Diagram (c), "Multiverse Engine", illustrates the runtime system that orchestrates the parallel execution of these reasoning paths. It consists of three main modules: Generator, Scheduler, and Memory Pool, arranged vertically. The Generator module (top) is an orange box containing the initial input: a parallelized goal and outline structure, represented as <Parallel><Goal>...<Outline>1...<Outline>2...<Goal>... . This input branches into two parallel paths, each encapsulated in a green box labeled <Path>1: ... </Path> and <Path>2: ... </Path>. These paths converge into a final conclusion box, which contains the text: <Conclusion>... Let's move back to sequential mode! , indicating the system's ability to conclude and revert to a standard sequential processing mode if needed.

The Scheduler module (middle) is a horizontally segmented box with three colored sections: an orange left section for detecting parallelism and goals, a green middle section for initiating parallel processes, and a peach-colored right section for concluding all paths. The scheduler performs several critical operations: it detects <Parallel> and <Goal> tags, starts the Map Phase, records the outlines, and then initiates parallel processing by prefilling specific paths for different tasks. For example, it prefills <Path>1 for Task 1 and <Path>2 for Task 2, before starting the Reduce Phase and concluding all paths. Icons accompany these actions: a pencil for detection, a globe for process finish, and a cluster of blocks for concluding.

The Memory Pool module (bottom) manages the memory state during parallel execution. It is divided into three sections: KV Cache Indices (left, peach-colored), Path 1 (middle, light green), and Path 2 (right, light green), each marked with a plus sign indicating addition or activation. An arrow labeled "Prefill" points from the Path 1 and Path 2 sections to a final section labeled Decoding Indices (peach-colored), indicating that the pre-filled path states are used to initialize the decoding process. The Memory Pool visually represents how the system maintains separate memory states for each active path while allowing them to be combined or merged during the decoding phase.

Together, these two diagrams demonstrate how the Multiverse framework enables efficient, parallel reasoning by decomposing tasks into multiple paths, scheduling their execution, and managing memory states independently for each path, ultimately converging to a unified conclusion. This design allows for rapid shifts from AR-LLMs (Autoregressive Large Language Models) to more flexible, multi-path reasoning architectures.

path_to_gt_image: images/NegoCollab A Common Representation Negotiation Approach for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 2: Overview of NegoCollab. Each agent shares features in the negotiated common representation space. Through the sender-receiver pairs, the features are mutually converted between local representation space and the common representation space, thereby enabling the mutual transformation of features across modalities and eliminating domain gaps.
golden_prompt:
The diagram illustrates the NegoCollab framework, a multi-agent collaborative perception system designed to enable feature sharing and mutual transformation between heterogeneous modalities (camera images and LiDAR point clouds) through a negotiated common representation space. The entire architecture is divided into three main sections: "Visualized Features" (top-left), "Collaborators" (top-right), and "Local" (bottom). These sections are visually separated by dotted-line boxes.

In the "Visualized Features" section, four labeled feature maps are displayed: ① Ego Feature (a blue-tinted point cloud visualization), ② Neb Feature (a purple, starburst-like pattern), ③ Neb Feature in Common Rep. (a green, structured grid overlay on a similar pattern), and ④ Neb Feature in Ego Rep. (a blue-tinted point cloud with a green overlay). These serve as visual references for the types of features processed.

The "Collaborators" section contains two agents: Neb1 (with a camera image input) and Neb2 (with a LiDAR point cloud input). Each agent's data passes through an "Encoder" module, producing encoded features F_{j→i}^{(m)} for Neb1 and F_{k→i}^{(l)} for Neb2. These features are then sent via "Sender" modules to the central "Common Rep. Space." The Common Rep. Space is a gray rectangular region containing four feature representations: P_i^{(m)}, P_j^{(n)}, P_k^{(n)}, and P_l^{(l)}. These are connected to the Senders via arrows labeled with wireless signal icons, indicating communication. A label "Feature Share" points to this space, emphasizing its role as a shared semantic space. The features from both collaborators are transformed into a common representation format for alignment.

The "Local" section at the bottom represents the ego vehicle’s processing pipeline. It begins with an "Ego" LiDAR point cloud input, which is encoded into a local feature F_i^{(m)}. This feature is then passed to a "Fusion" module, which combines it with received features from the collaborators (F_j^{(m)} and F_k^{(m)}) after they have been transformed into the local representation space. The fusion process produces a "Fused Feature" G_i^{(m)}. This fused feature is fed into a "Head" module, which outputs "Detection Results" (visualized as a black-and-white image with red bounding boxes around detected objects). The "Local Prompt" is generated by a "Receiver" module, which receives features from the Common Rep. Space and converts them into the local representation space before feeding them into the Fusion module. The Receiver also sends a prompt back to the Sender in the Collaborators section, completing the bidirectional communication loop. The entire system enables cross-modal feature negotiation and alignment, allowing each agent to understand and interpret features from other agents' perspectives, thereby reducing domain gaps.

visual_intent: Figure 3: Overview of our NEURIPT, which comprises Amplitude-Aware Masked Pretraining (AAMP), 3D Electrode Embedding, Progressive Mixture-of-Experts (PMoE), and Intra-Inter Lobe Pooling (IILP) for fine-tuning. See Figure 4 for details on the IILP module.
golden_prompt: The diagram illustrates the architecture of NEURIPT, a neural network model for EEG data processing, divided into two main phases: pre-training and downstream fine-tuning. The left side details the pre-training phase, starting with an input of multi-channel EEG signals represented as waveforms. These signals undergo Amplitude-Aware Masking (AAMP), where masking is applied based on signal amplitude, indicated by a red arrow labeled L_AAMP pointing from the masked waveform to the decoder block. The masked EEG signals are then fed into a 3D Electrode Embedding layer, which generates embeddings for each electrode position in 3D space. This embedding feeds into a stack of N Encoder Blocks, each containing a Progressive MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) module, a Spatial Attention mechanism, and a Temporal Attention mechanism, followed by Layer Normalization. The encoder output is passed to a Decoder Block, which includes a Feed-Forward Network (FFN) and a Transformer-based Self-Attention module (TSA). The decoder reconstructs the original EEG signals, forming a feedback loop with the AAMP module. The entire pre-training stage is labeled 'Pre-training'. The right side of the diagram shows the downstream fine-tuning phase. The output from the decoder's FFN and TSA is routed through a 'Downstream Fine-tuning' pathway to an 'Intra-Inter Lobe Pooling' (IILP) module. This module contains five distinct lobes: Frontal, Occipital, Temporal L, Temporal R, and Parietal, each represented by a colored box. These lobes are connected to a central circular node labeled C, indicating a fusion or classification output. The IILP module is further linked to two parallel blocks, Block 1 and Block N, each representing a different level of the model hierarchy. Each block contains multiple expert modules (illustrated as cartoon characters) and a router module (represented by a green bar chart). For example, Block 1 has Expert 1, Expert 2, and a Shared Expert, while Block N has Expert 1, Expert 2, ..., Expert n+1, and a Shared Expert. The router directs inputs to specific experts based on routing decisions. The entire structure is enclosed within dashed boxes labeled 'Block 1' and 'Block N', indicating modular components. The diagram uses color coding: pink for MoE modules, blue for attention mechanisms, yellow for TSA, green for routers, and various colors for lobe representations. Arrows indicate data flow, with solid arrows for direct connections and dotted arrows for routing or feedback paths. The overall layout follows a top-down flow from input EEG signals to final output C, with branching pathways for pre-training and fine-tuning.

path_to_gt_image: images/No Object Is an Island Enhancing 3D Semantic Segmentation Generalization with Diffusion Models_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 2: A brief illustration of our proposed framework. First, we aggregate semantic information of objects within the scene from diffusion features to form the object agent queries. Next, we propose a dual-query mechanism to eliminate local visual details from the object agent queries, preventing interference with 3D semantic representation. Finally, the optimized object agent queries are used as an interface to infuse inter-object semantic dependencies into the 3D representation, guiding the model to learn domain-invariant features.
golden_prompt:
The figure presents a three-part architectural diagram illustrating a cross-modal framework for enhancing 3D semantic understanding using object agent queries derived from diffusion models. The layout is divided into three horizontal sections labeled (a), (b), and (c), each describing a sequential phase of the methodology.

In section (a), titled "Construction of Object Agent Queries", the process begins with a source image on the left, which feeds into a pre-trained encoder to produce a latent vector z0. This latent is then passed through a diffusion model alongside added noise, producing aggregated instance semantics. These semantics are further processed by a "Dual-queries Design" module, which generates multiple types of queries: 2D object agent queries (light blue), 2D auxiliary queries (dark blue), and 3D object agent queries (orange). A legend clarifies these query types. The output of this design is fed into a "Principal Component Extraction" block, which produces q_ins_pc, representing quantized object agent queries.

Section (b), "Dual-queries Consistency Scheme", shows how the quantized queries are refined. The input q_ins_pc flows into an MLP layer, followed by a consistency loss function L_consist, which ensures alignment across queries. The output is again q_ins_pc, now refined. This section also includes a parallel pathway for cross-modal semantic alignment, where features from the 3D side are aligned with the 2D queries via linear transformations and MLPs, ensuring semantic coherence between modalities.

Section (c), "Cross-modal Semantic Enhancement", depicts the final stage where the refined queries guide 3D feature learning. A source point cloud is processed by a backbone network with layers 1 to L, generating a 3D feature map q_3D. This feature undergoes two rounds of "Feature Refinement" modules, each with shared weights and supervised losses L_sup and L_sup^s. The refined features are then decoded to produce a segmentation label via a convolutional layer and loss L_seg. The entire 3D pipeline is connected back to the dual-query scheme via cross-modal alignment, creating a feedback loop that integrates object-level semantic information into the 3D representation. The diagram uses color-coded blocks (yellow for backbone, orange for refinement, green for alignment) and arrows to indicate data flow, with loss functions shown as labeled boxes. The overall structure emphasizes a cascaded refinement process from image-based queries to 3D semantic enhancement.

path_to_gt_image: images/Noisy Multi-Label Learning through Co-Occurrence-Aware Diffusion_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: The illustration of the co-occurrence-aware diffusion model. The example comes from the MS-COCO dataset, where the label set has been corrupted to $\{ P e r s o n , \qquad , B o a t \}$ . The true co-occurrence probability of the label pair $<$ Elephant, $B o a t >$ is very low, so our intuition is to constrain the learning weight of this pair during the reverse process. The pseudo-clean label set $\{ P e r s o n , D o g , B o a t \}$ , estimated through latent neighborhood space, is more suitable as the starting point $\mathbf { y } _ { 0 }$ for label diffusion after being transformed into matrix form.
golden_prompt: The diagram illustrates a co-occurrence-aware diffusion-based model for multi-label image generation, structured in two main horizontal sections: an upper 'Conditional Information' section and a lower 'Diffusion-based Model' section. The upper section processes noisy labels using a latent neighborhood space to derive pseudo-clean labels, while the lower section applies a diffusion process to generate clean labels. The entire diagram is enclosed by a dashed green border labeled 'Instance', containing a central photograph of a person in a kayak with a dog, which serves as the input instance. From this image, three noisy multi-labels — 'Person', 'Elephant', and 'Boat' — are extracted via dashed arrows, each represented by a yellow rectangle. These labels feed into a 'Latent Neighborhood Space' module, depicted as a white box with a blue central node connected to multiple colored nodes (red, orange, teal, light blue) by lines, symbolizing relationships among labels. Below this module is a blue rectangular block labeled 'Co-Occurrence-Aware', indicating the mechanism that adjusts label weights based on co-occurrence probabilities. The output of this module is a 'Pseudo-clean Multi-labels' block, also composed of yellow rectangles, now showing corrected labels: 'Person', 'Dog', and 'Boat'. A purple cube labeled 'Matrixing' transforms these pseudo-clean labels into a matrix format before feeding them into the diffusion model. The lower section, labeled 'Diffusion-based Model', is enclosed in a dashed orange border. It shows a forward process (left to right) and a reverse process (right to left), both represented by arrows. The forward process begins at 'y_t ~ N(0, I)' (a multivariate normal distribution) and evolves through intermediate states to 'y_0' (the final clean label vector). The reverse process, governed by the conditional probability p_theta(y_{t-1} | y_t, x, t), starts from 'y_t' and moves backward to 'y_0'. The reverse process is explicitly labeled with the equation p_theta(y_{t-1} | y_t, x, t) and q(y_t | y_{t-1}), indicating the model's probabilistic inference. The diffusion process is visually represented by bar charts transitioning from noisy to clean distributions, with intermediate steps indicated by ellipses. The entire diagram uses color coding: green for the instance and conditional information, orange for the diffusion model, and blue for the co-occurrence-aware component. The caption explains that the example uses MS-COCO data, where the label set was corrupted to include 'Person', 'Elephant', and 'Boat', but the true co-occurrence between 'Elephant' and 'Boat' is low, so the model constrains the learning weight of such pairs. The pseudo-clean labels are derived from the latent neighborhood space and serve as the optimal starting point y_0 for label diffusion.

path_to_gt_image: images/OMiSO Adaptive optimization of state-dependent brain stimulation to shape neural population states_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: Goal of OMiSO and experimental paradigm. (A) OMiSO finds a stimulation pattern (grid representing an electrode array, where the stimulated electrodes are indicated by orange cells) to drive neural population activity toward a target state (pink star) given a pre-stimulation state (black dots). For different pre-stimulation states (Pre-stim state 1 vs. Pre-stim state 2), OMiSO selects different stimulation patterns (green bolt vs. yellow bolt) to achieve the same target state. OMiSO updates the selected stimulation patterns from early (left panel, green bolt) to late (right panel, orange bolt) in an experimental session to achieve the target state. This is necessitated by the fact that the stimulation pattern that achieved the target state early in the session (left panel, green bolt) no longer does so late in the session (right panel, green bolt). (B) Experimental setup. Top: The monkey performed a memory-guided saccade task (Section S3) while spiking activity was recorded from a multi-electrode array implanted in PFC. Pre-uStim neural activity (gray bars) was recorded over five consecutive $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ bins. During the $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ computation period (blue unfilled bar), the system chose a uStim pattern, which was then applied for $4 0 \mathrm { m s }$ (orange bar). Post-uStim neural activity (pink bar) was measured starting $1 0 \mathrm { m s }$ after stimulation offset. Bottom: neural population activity was analyzed in a low-d (in our experiments, 5-d) latent space.
golden_prompt:
The figure illustrates the OMiSO (Optimal Motor Stimulation Optimization) method for driving neural populations toward a target state during a memory-guided saccade task in primates. It is divided into two main panels, A and B, each depicting distinct but complementary aspects of the methodology.

Panel A demonstrates the adaptive nature of OMiSO across time within an experimental session. It contains two side-by-side 3D plots labeled 'Early in a session' (left) and 'Late in a session' (right). Each plot represents a 3D coordinate system with axes labeled 'Neuron 1', 'Neuron 2', and 'Neuron 3'. In both plots, a 'Target brain state z' is marked by a pink star at coordinates (z1, z2, z3) along the respective axes. Two distinct 'Pre-stim state' points are shown as black dots: 'Pre-stim state 1 z' and 'Pre-stim state 2 z'. These represent the initial neural population states before stimulation. From each pre-stim state, a colored arrow (bolt) indicates the stimulation pattern chosen by OMiSO to drive the population toward the target state. In the left panel ('Early'), a green bolt originates from 'Pre-stim state 1 z' and points toward the target. In the right panel ('Late'), a different stimulation pattern is shown: an orange bolt originates from 'Pre-stim state 1 z' (now shifted slightly) and points toward the target. The visual contrast between the green and orange bolts emphasizes that OMiSO dynamically adjusts its stimulation strategy as the session progresses, because the same stimulation pattern effective early on becomes less effective later.

Panel B details the experimental setup and data analysis pipeline. The top section shows a timeline of the task phases: 'Pre-uStim' (gray bars, 50 ms duration), 'uStim' (orange bar, 40 ms), and 'Post-uStim' (pink bar, 10 ms). Above this timeline, a schematic of the monkey performing the task is shown alongside a representation of the 'Utah array' (a grid of electrodes) implanted in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). The 'Memory period' is indicated below the timeline, showing the interval between stimulus presentation and the saccade response. The bottom section of Panel B presents a 2D latent space plot with axes labeled 'Latent dim 1' and 'Latent dim 2'. A curved trajectory of gray dots represents the evolution of neural activity over time. The 'Pre-uStim state' is marked at the start of the curve, followed by the 'uStim' event (indicated by a yellow lightning bolt) and the resulting 'Post-uStim state' (a pink dot). The 'Target activity state' is marked as a pink star, and an arrow labeled 'Error' connects it to the 'Post-uStim state', indicating the discrepancy between the desired and actual outcome. The entire figure conveys that OMiSO operates in a low-dimensional latent space to compute optimal stimulation patterns that minimize this error and guide neural activity toward a predefined target state.

path_to_gt_image: images/OSKAR Omnimodal Self-supervised Knowledge Abstraction and Representation_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 2: OSKAR Architecture. Multimodal tokens (e.g., video, skeleton, text) are projected into a shared space and split into two branches: (1) a fusion encoder processes visible tokens to produce fused representations; (2) modality-specific target encoders generate target embeddings. A predictor estimates masked representations from fused tokens, supervised via MSE loss against targets. Target encoders are updated via EMA of the fusion encoder and are used exclusively in fine-tuning.
golden_prompt: The figure illustrates the OSKAR architecture, a multimodal model processing video, skeleton, and text inputs through projection modules, a fusion encoder, and target encoders, with prediction and loss components. The layout is divided into three main vertical sections: input tokens on the left, a top fusion branch with an EMA update mechanism in the center, and a right prediction and loss branch. Inputs include video tokens (red), skeleton tokens (yellow), and text tokens (blue), shown as stacked rectangles with corresponding color-coded legend. These tokens feed into three parallel projection blocks — Vision Projection (red), Motion Projection (yellow), Language Projection (blue) — each transforming their respective token type into a unified representation. These projections converge into a large 'Fusion Encoder' block (gray rectangle labeled f_θ), which generates a fused representation H. This fusion output feeds into three predictors — Vision Predictor, Motion Predictor, Lang. Predictor — each producing a predicted output Y^p. These predictions are compared against ground truth targets Y^t via MSE Loss modules, one per modality (red, yellow, blue), forming the supervision loop. Below the fusion encoder, a separate branch contains 'Target Encoders' — Vision Target Encoder, Motion Target Encoder, Language Target Encoder — which are updated via Exponential Moving Average (EMA) from the fusion encoder's parameters. A centralized clustering method (e.g., $\mathbf { k }$ -means) is applied to the global distance matrix to produce the final clustering result $\pi ^ { * }$ .

visual_intent: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PANDA. As shown in the figure, upon receiving a user-defined query, PANDA first performs environment perception and plans a scene-adaptive detection strategy. When encountering ambiguous cases, PANDA enters a reflection phase, revising its plan and invoking external tools to refine the decision. This input feeds into two parallel processing branches: VLM Perception and VLM Reasoning. The VLM Reasoning branch generates initial reasoning results (Status: Normal/Abnormal/Insufficient, Score, Reason) based on this input. The derivative term adds awareness of real-time tendencies, accelerating descent while reducing overshoot. Together, these mechanisms enhance both sampling speed and quality.

visual_intent: Figure 2: The pipeline of our Point-MaDi framework. The encoder adopts a center diffusion process, where noise is added to the centers of both visible and masked patches. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) maps the noisy centers to positional embeddings, and both these and visible patch embeddings are input to a transformer to predict the clean centers. The decoder performs a patch diffusion process, conditioned on the visible tokens and the predicted centers, to progressively denoise and reconstruct the masked patches. The chamfer distance guides the patch reconstruction, while the stop gradient (SG) operation prevents leakage of ground-truth masked patch positions during pre-training.

The input point set PPS is processed through KNN to form mini-PointNet blocks, which feed into a sequence of blue rectangular 'Encoder' modules. These encoders progressively reduce the dimensionality of the point cloud representations C_T^m, C_{T-1}^m, ..., C_1^m, until reaching a final representation C_0^m. This final representation passes through a gray 'Pos Embed Layer' module, followed by a stop gradient (SG) operator, indicating that gradients from this point onward are blocked. Section (b), 'Patch Diffusion Process', depicts a reverse diffusion process. It begins with a noisy point cloud P_0^m, which is compared to a target point cloud via Chamfer Distance. An FC Layer processes the initial point cloud, feeding into a series of purple 'Decoder' modules. These decoders progressively refine the point cloud representations P_1^m, P_2^m, ..., P_T^m, ultimately reconstructing the original point cloud. The reconstructed output is compared against the target using Chamfer Distance. Section (c), 'Encoder Module', details the internal structure of the encoder. It receives inputs C_{T-1}^m and C_{T-1}^v, which are passed through a 'Pos Embed Layer'. The outputs are combined via addition operations (+) and fed into a sequence of Transformer Blocks (labeled L_1, ..., L_n). Each Transformer Block contains self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms, followed by MLP layers. The final output is C_{T-2}^m. Section (d), 'Transformer Block', provides a detailed view of the transformer architecture. It includes a 'Shared Layer Norm' module, followed by two types of attention mechanisms: 'Self-Atttn' and 'Cross-Atttn'. These attention modules are connected to a 'Shared MLP' layer, which processes the outputs. The entire block is designed to handle multi-modal inputs and produce contextualized outputs. The color coding in the figure indicates different types of embeddings: blue for PE^m (masked patch positional embeddings), teal for PE^v (visible patch positional embeddings), gray for E^m (masked patch embeddings), green for E^v (visible patch embeddings), orange for T^m (masked token embeddings), and pink for T^v (visible token embeddings). path_to_gt_image: images/Preventing Shortcuts in Adapter Training via Providing the Shortcuts_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 3: Method. The Shortcut-Rerouting (SR)-Module serves as a generic shortcut adapter that can take various forms—such as a ControlNet, LoRA, or IP-Adapter—depending on the confounding factor being addressed (e.g., pose, distribution, or style). Illustrated here is the case of SR with ControlNet, where pose and expression cues are explicitly rerouted via the ControlNet during adapter training. At inference time, the ControlNet is removed, restoring independent pose and expression control from the text prompt alone.

The figure presents a two-part workflow illustrating a 'Shortcut-Rerouted Training' and 'Inference' process for a T2I (Text-to-Image) model, with a focus on how an SR-Module (e.g., ControlNet) is used during training and then removed at inference. The layout is horizontally split into two main sections labeled '1. Shortcut-Rerouted Training' and '2. Inference', each with distinct visual modules and connections.

In the first section, 'Shortcut-Rerouted Training', a noisy image (left) is fed into a central gray trapezoidal module labeled 'T2I'. This T2I module receives two inputs: one from an 'SR-Module' (labeled 'e.g., ControlNet') and another from an 'Adapter' module. The SR-Module is depicted as a beige trapezoid with a small icon showing a person's face and pose, and it has a padlock symbol above it, indicating it is active during training. The Adapter is also a beige trapezoid, marked with a flame icon, suggesting it processes or modifies the input. Both modules feed into the T2I module via upward-pointing arrows. The output of the T2I module is a clean, high-quality image of a person with green hair and glasses, standing against a sunset cityscape.

Below the T2I module, there are three example images arranged horizontally: the leftmost shows the same person but in profile, the middle shows the person facing forward, and the rightmost shows the person in a different pose. These images are connected by curved arrows to the SR-Module and Adapter, indicating they are used as training examples. A large black circular annotation surrounds two of these images (the profile and forward-facing ones), with red 'X' marks over them, suggesting they are being filtered or ignored during training. An arrow loops back from this annotation to the Adapter, implying feedback or selection based on the filtered examples.

In the second section, 'Inference', the setup is simplified. The T2I module is again shown as a gray trapezoid, but now it only receives input from the 'Adapter' module, which is depicted as a beige trapezoid with no additional icons. Below the Adapter, there is a single image of the person smiling directly at the camera, which is presumably the reference image for generating the final output. An arrow points from this image to the Adapter, indicating it is used to guide the generation. The output of the T2I module is a final image of the person standing in profile, gazing to the left, as specified by the text caption above the T2I module: '"standing in profile, gazing to the left"'.

The overall structure highlights the contrast between training and inference: during training, the SR-Module and Adapter work together to reroute specific cues (like pose and expression) through the T2I model, while at inference, the SR-Module is removed, allowing the T2I model to independently generate the desired output based solely on the text prompt and the Adapter's guidance.

path_to_gt_image: images/ProSpero Active Learning for Robust Protein Design Beyond Wild-Type Neighborhoods_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: Overview of PROSPERO. Each active learning iteration begins with training a surrogate model on the current dataset (A). The surrogate is then used to identify fitness-relevant residues within the top sequence (B), which are subsequently masked, yielding partially masked sequences (C). EvoDiff, guided by the surrogate, completes these sequences to generate new candidates $( \mathrm { D } )$ , which are evaluated by the oracle and added to the dataset (E).
golden_prompt: The diagram illustrates the workflow of PROSPERO, an active learning framework for protein sequence design. The process is cyclical and consists of five main stages labeled (A) through (E), arranged vertically from top to bottom with arrows indicating flow direction. At the top left, a database icon labeled 'Dataset D_n' serves as the input source. An arrow labeled 'x_start' points from this database to a vertical stack of five horizontal bars, each containing the amino acid 'Ala', representing initial sequences. To the right of this stack, a column of five circular icons shows evaluation results: two red 'X's at the top and bottom, and three green checkmarks in between. These icons feed into a box labeled '(C) Search space constraints', which contains three horizontal bars with '[MASK]' placeholders, defining allowed residue types based on charge: positive (R,K,H), negative (D,E), and neutral (N,Q,S,...). A dashed box next to this section details the masking rules. Below the constraint box, a rounded rectangle labeled '(D) Sequential Monte Carlo guidance' receives input from the constraints and connects via an arrow to another rounded rectangle labeled 'EvoDiff'. EvoDiff generates candidate sequences, which are then passed to a graph-like structure composed of interconnected blue nodes representing a probabilistic sampling process. This graph feeds into a light green rounded rectangle labeled '(E) Oracle evaluation', which evaluates the generated candidates. The output of the oracle flows back to the left side of the diagram, where it is added to the original dataset D_n, completing the cycle. A diagonal arrow labeled '(A) Proxy training' originates from the dataset D_n and points to a central yellow rounded rectangle labeled 'Proxy f_θ', indicating that the proxy model is trained on the current dataset. Another arrow labeled '(B) Residue selection' points from the proxy model to the sequence stack, signifying that the proxy identifies relevant residues for masking. The proxy model also has a feedback loop to the constraint box, suggesting it influences or refines the search space. The entire diagram uses consistent visual elements: rounded rectangles for modules, arrows for data flow, and distinct colors (yellow for proxy, green for oracle, light blue for EvoDiff) to differentiate components. Text labels are clearly placed near each module or step, and the layout emphasizes the iterative nature of the algorithm.

path_to_gt_image: images/Progressive Inference-Time Annealing of Diffusion Models for Sampling from Boltzmann Densities_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: Illustration of the proposed PITA framework combining two complementary processes: temperature annealing of the target Boltzmann density and the diffusion process applied to the collected samples. Annealed inference allows for decreasing the temperature (increasing $\beta$ ) of a trained diffusion model, thus generating samples from the annealed target. These samples can be reused for training a lower-temperature diffusion model.
golden_prompt: The figure illustrates the PITA framework, which combines temperature annealing and a diffusion process to generate samples from an annealed target distribution. The global layout is a horizontal timeline along the x-axis labeled 'τ', ranging from τ=1 on the left to τ=0 on the right, representing the progression of the diffusion process. Along this timeline, multiple probability density functions (PDFs) are plotted as bell-shaped curves, evolving from broad, low-peak distributions at τ=1 to sharp, high-peak distributions at τ=0. A diagonal axis labeled 'β' runs from bottom-left to top-right, indicating increasing temperature annealing, with annotations π(x)^β=0.1 at the lower end and π(x)^β=1 at the upper end. The curves are color-coded by temperature: orange-red for low β (τ=1), transitioning to magenta-purple for higher β (τ=0). A legend box in the upper-left corner defines four key components using distinct arrow styles: dashed-dotted arrows for 'Inference-time annealing', dotted arrows for 'Noising of samples', dash-dot arrows for 'Diffusion inference', and solid arrows for 'PITA'. The main workflow is shown via arrows connecting the PDFs: starting from τ=1, a solid arrow labeled 'PITA' points to a subsequent PDF, indicating the application of the PITA method. From there, a dotted arrow labeled 'Diffusion inference' leads to another PDF, showing the diffusion step. A dashed-dotted arrow labeled 'Noising of samples' connects back to an earlier stage, illustrating sample re-use. A dashed arrow labeled 'Inference-time annealing' points from the final high-β PDF toward the β-axis, emphasizing the annealing effect. The entire sequence visually demonstrates how samples generated at a lower temperature (τ=1, β=0.1) are progressively refined through diffusion and annealing to produce samples from a higher-temperature target (τ=0, β=1).

The first stage involves sampling from a Gaussian distribution N(0,1) to initialize latent variables, denoted as z_T. This initial sample undergoes multiple PRLD steps, represented by a sequence of arrows labeled "Multiple PRLD Steps" leading to intermediate latent states z_t and z_{t-2}. The MICP mechanism also includes components labeled S_θ and D, connected via arrows indicating transformations. The LMG mechanism is shown on the right side of the diagram, involving operations such as sample generation, fusion loss (L_fusion), gradient descent (G), and Sobel operator application. It includes components labeled ξ, S_θ, D, and R, with arrows indicating data flow and loss computation. The final step involves combining the processed latent representation with a regularization term R, which is added via a plus sign before being passed to the output layer. The output is visualized as a composite image labeled "Output," showing a synthesized result derived from the infrared and visible inputs. The entire architecture is organized into distinct sections: input sources, initialization, iterative PRLD steps, MICP and LMG mechanisms, and final output generation, all interconnected through directional arrows indicating the flow of information and computations.

Each branch contains multiple nodes (represented by images of a robotic arm interacting with a microwave) annotated with timestamps [o₀], [o₉], [o₁₄], etc., indicating the state of the robot at different points in time. The final node in each branch shows completion: at [o₁₄], the steak is placed inside, and the task is complete. The framework uses two types of operators: φ (phi), which represents a transition or transformation between states, and ψ (psi), which denotes a decision point or subtask completion. These operators are visually represented as boxes with arrows connecting them to subsequent nodes. The φ operator appears at the top of each branch, indicating the initial state transition, while ψ appears at intermediate steps, marking subtask milestones. The arrows indicate the flow of control and state transitions, with solid lines showing direct progression and dotted lines indicating optional or conditional paths. The figure also includes task progress indicators (e.g., 'Task progress: 0%', '40%', '100%') to show how the robot’s actions contribute to completing the overall goal. The visual style is consistent across all nodes, featuring a white robotic arm against a kitchen background with a microwave, ensuring clarity and focus on the task decomposition process. The overall structure emphasizes recursion and modularity, allowing the system to reason about long-term goals by breaking them into manageable, temporally compact subproblems.

path_to_gt_image: images/RadZero Similarity-Based Cross-Attention for Explainable Vision-Language Alignment in Chest X-ray with Zero-Shot Multi-Task Capability_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 3: The overall framework of RadZero. (a) Finding-sentence extraction using an LLM. (b) Computation of the similarity logit, $l _ { i j } ^ { n }$ , between image $I _ { i }$ and finding-sentence $S _ { j _ { - } } ^ { n }$ . W-sum and cos-sim denote weighted sum and cosine similarity, respectively. (c) Computation of MP-NCE loss $( \mathcal { L } _ { I } )$ and InfoNCE loss $( \mathcal { L } _ { T } )$ from the similarity logit matrix. (d) Zero-shot inference pipeline.
golden_prompt:
The figure presents the overall framework of RadZero, divided into four main sections labeled (a), (b), (c), and (d), each describing a distinct component of the model's architecture. Section (a) illustrates the process of extracting finding-sentences from radiology reports using a Large Language Model (LLM). A sample radiology report is shown as input text, which is processed by the LLM to output a list of finding-sentences, such as 'There is left retrocardiac opacity' or 'There may be atelectasis'. These sentences are then used as targets for the vision model.

Section (b) details the core vision-language alignment mechanism. It begins with a radiology image, denoted as I_i, which is fed into a Vision Encoder (represented as a blue box with a snowflake icon). The encoded visual features are passed through Transformer Layers (pink box) to produce a Vision Token Sequence composed of L patches, visually represented as vertical pink bars. Simultaneously, a finding-sentence S_j^n is input into a Text Encoder (light green box), generating a Text Embedding. The vision token sequence and text embedding are then combined via two operations: first, a weighted sum (W-sum) operation, depicted as a horizontal arrow labeled 'w-sum', producing a Vision Embedding; second, a cosine similarity (cos-sim) computation, shown as a downward arrow labeled 'cos-sim', which yields Similarity Scores (orange squares). These scores are then used to compute the final Similarity Logit l_ij^n, represented as a yellow square.

Section (c) describes the training objective based on the similarity logit matrix. This matrix, labeled 'Similarity Logit Matrix', is structured as a grid where rows represent images I_1 to I_B and columns represent finding-sentences S_1^n to S_N^n. Each cell contains a '+' symbol indicating positive similarity, with some cells highlighted in yellow to emphasize selected pairs. Two losses are computed from this matrix: the InfoNCE Loss (L_T), indicated by a red arrow pointing right, and the MP-NCE Loss (L_I), indicated by a red arrow pointing down. The total loss L is defined as the sum of these two components: L = L_I + L_T.

Section (d) outlines the zero-shot inference pipeline. Starting from a single similarity probability l_ij^n (yellow square), it undergoes a sigmoid transformation σ to produce a normalized similarity score. This score is then used for Zero-Shot Classification (red arrow labeled 'Inference'). The process continues by constructing a Patch-Level Similarity Map M_ij^n from multiple patch-level similarities, followed by interpolation & σ to generate a Pixel-Level Similarity Map M_ij^n (visualized as a heatmap). Finally, this map is used for Zero-Shot Grounding and Zero-Shot Segmentation (red arrow labeled 'Inference'), enabling pixel-level localization of medical findings without requiring task-specific training data. The entire framework integrates vision, language, and contrastive learning to enable robust zero-shot performance in radiology interpretation.

path_to_gt_image: images/RankSEG-RMA An Efficient Segmentation Algorithm via Reciprocal Moment Approximation_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: Comparison of Argmax-prob and RankSEG-RMA. (a) Argmax-prob: each pixel is predicted to the class with the highest probability. (b) RankSEG-RMA: segmentation masks $\hat { \overline { { \mathcal { I } } } } _ { c } ^ { + }$ for each class are obtained independently; non-overlapping parts $\widehat { \cal T } _ { c }$ are accepted, while overlaps ${ \widehat { \cal T } } ^ { \mathrm { o v e r l a p } }$ are resolved by applying argmax over RMA-scores.
golden_prompt: The diagram illustrates a comparative workflow between two segmentation prediction methods: Argmax-prob and RankSEG-RMA, presented side-by-side within a single horizontal layout. At the top, a header bar visually separates the two methods. On the left, 'Class A' is represented by a teal rectangle and 'Class B' by a salmon rectangle, indicating the two classes being segmented. An arrow labeled 'Argmax-prob' points from this header to a box labeled 'RankSEG-RMA', which then connects via a blue arrow to the final output stage. The main body of the diagram is vertically divided into two parallel processing paths: one for Argmax-prob (left side) and one for RankSEG-RMA (right side), both starting from the same input probability map. The input probability map, labeled 'Probability \hat{p}', is a 4x4 grid of numerical values (e.g., 0.05, 0.48, 0.90, etc.) displayed in black text on a white background. From this grid, two branches emerge: one leading to a binary segmentation mask for Class A (teal square with a white cross) and another to a binary segmentation mask for Class B (salmon square with a salmon cross). These masks are labeled \hat{\mathcal{T}}_A^+ and \hat{\mathcal{T}}_B^+, respectively, with the superscript '+' indicating positive predictions. The Argmax-prob path continues from these masks to a final prediction image (teal cross on a teal background) labeled 'Argmax-prob Prediction (IoU^T = 61.69)', where IoU^T is shown in purple text. The RankSEG-RMA path, however, proceeds differently. After generating the initial masks \hat{\mathcal{T}}_A^+ and \hat{\mathcal{T}}_B^+, a step labeled '(1) Accept non-overlaps (2) Discard overlaps (3) Compute RMA-scores' is applied. This leads to a central RMA-scores matrix, which is a 4x4 grid of red numbers (e.g., 1.33, 2.09, 2.34) on a green background. Below this matrix, mathematical formulas define the overlap region \hat{\mathcal{T}}_{overlap} = \hat{\mathcal{T}}_A^+ \cap \hat{\mathcal{T}}_B^+ and the resulting non-overlapping regions \hat{\mathcal{T}}_A = \hat{\mathcal{T}}_A^+ \setminus \hat{\mathcal{T}}_{overlap} and \hat{\mathcal{T}}_B = \hat{\mathcal{T}}_B^+ \setminus \hat{\mathcal{T}}_{overlap}. From the RMA-scores matrix, an arrow labeled \delta_j = \arg\max_c \hat{p}_{c,j} \forall j \in [d] points to the final RankSEG-RMA prediction image (salmon cross on a salmon background), labeled 'RankSEG-RMA Prediction (IoU^T = 63.04)' in blue text. The entire diagram uses color coding: teal for Class A, salmon for Class B, green for intermediate matrices, and white for background elements. Text labels are primarily black or colored to match their associated components. Arrows are solid lines with arrowheads indicating directionality, and some arrows are colored (purple for Argmax-prob, blue for RankSEG-RMA) to distinguish the two workflows. The diagram's purpose is to demonstrate that RankSEG-RMA achieves a higher IoU score (63.04) than Argmax-prob (61.69) by resolving overlaps using RMA-scores rather than simply selecting the class with the highest probability per pixel.

path_to_gt_image: images/ReAgent-V A Reward-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Video Understanding_diagram.jpg
visual_intent: Figure 1: Overview of the ReAgent-V framework: The system first selects relevant video frames based on the input question through the entropy-calibrated frame selection module and invokes various tools from the tool factory to assist in reasoning. The target agent generates an initial answer using the selected tools and input context, which is then critically evaluated by the critic agent through questioning and scoring, ultimately producing a comprehensive feedback report. The target agent can then revise its answer from three perspectives—conservative, neutral, and aggressive—based on the report and updated context. In addition to generating standard reasoning outputs, high-scoring data identified during the reflection process based on the feedback report is stored for training algorithms such as SFT, DPO, and GRPO, thereby further enhancing model performance.
